subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Planning Fallacy
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Planning Fallacy.

hook.text: The Sydney Opera House was budgeted for four years. It took fourteen. Every planner thought this time was different.

buildup.text: Kahneman found people predict project times by best-case scenarios and ignore base rates of delay.

discovery.text: The planning fallacy: we underestimate time, cost, and risk while overestimating our own efficiency.

twist.text: Even knowing about this bias barely helps. People who learn it still underestimate their own plans.

climax.text: The fix: use reference class forecasting. Ask how long similar projects took, not how long yours feels.

punchline.text: Your plan is not special. Check the base rate.

quiz.question: What is the planning fallacy?
options: Underestimating time and cost based on best-case thinking
Refusing to plan ahead at all

details.summary: The planning fallacy is the systematic tendency to underestimate the time, cost, and risk of future projects while overestimating their benefits. People plan for best-case scenarios, ignore historical base rates, and remain optimistic despite a personal history of overruns.
details.whyItMatters: The planning fallacy costs billions annually in budget overruns, missed deadlines, and failed projects. From home renovations to mega-infrastructure projects, the pattern is universal: initial estimates are almost always too optimistic.
takeaways: Projects routinely exceed initial time and cost estimates by 50 to 100 percent
People use the inside view of their specific plan rather than base rates
Reference class forecasting is the most effective corrective technique

faq.question: Why do people fall for the planning fallacy despite repeated experience?
faq.answer: Each new project feels unique, so people use the inside view: they imagine their specific plan working smoothly. They fail to consult their own history of overruns, treating each project as a fresh start where past mistakes are irrelevant.

faq.question: What is the best way to create more accurate project estimates?
faq.answer: Use reference class forecasting: find similar past projects and base your estimate on their actual outcomes. If similar projects typically run 50 percent over budget, add 50 percent to your estimate regardless of how different you think your project is.
